messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mereana Te Rangi is a 77-year-old Māori American surgeon who had spent decades moving through hospitals with a kind of disciplined certainty, the operating room feeling more familiar to her than her own living room after her divorce. The illness that altered her life began abruptly during what had been an ordinary workday. She remembers scrubbing in, the sharp antiseptic smell, the fluorescent brightness over stainless steel, and then a sudden cascade of bodily sensations that made no sense to her at first—weakness, a rush of fear, the conviction that something inside her was failing. What followed is not a coherent story in her mind but a series of jagged images: the cold rail of a gurney against her forearm, a monitor sounding somewhere too fast, a colleague’s face suspended above her with an expression she had never seen directed at her before. Other stretches are simply absent. She says there are entire parts of the episode she cannot retrieve no matter how long she sits with it, while a few moments remain painfully exact.

In the months afterward, those disconnected fragments became strangely powerful. Mereana found herself going over the event repeatedly, trying to understand why it had happened to her of all people. She had always been the physician, never the patient, and the gaps in her memory made the whole experience feel unfinished, intolerably unresolved. Because she could not form a single continuous account, she kept circling the pieces she did have, searching for meaning in them, wondering whether the illness had exposed some hidden weakness or marked a turning point she should be able to explain. At the same time, she forced herself toward a rigid kind of optimism, telling herself to think only positive thoughts and refusing to dwell openly on how frightened she still was. The effort had a brittle quality, more suppression than comfort, as if staying relentlessly “upbeat” might keep the missing parts from breaking through.

These fractured memories also changed how she saw herself. The blank spaces unsettled her as much as the vivid images, because they made her feel unlike the precise, authoritative woman she had always known herself to be. Mereana had built an identity around steadiness under pressure, detailed recall, and mastery of the body’s vulnerabilities. Now she found herself saying that the person she had become was unrecognizable to her. She could not trust her own mind to hold the event properly, and from there it was not a large step to feeling that she no longer knew who she was. Something in her faith—in life’s order, in the reliability of the roles she had lived by—had given way during the illness and had not returned.

Her attempts to manage this only tightened the problem. Because hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations now stirred up the clearest sensory shards of the episode, she began avoiding them whenever she could, an extraordinary shift for someone whose profession had always placed her at the center of medical life. At work she reduced her hours and delegated more of the pre- and postoperative contact she once handled herself, lingering outside examination areas until she had to enter, feeling her body tense at the sound of wheels in the corridor or the sight of a stretcher being pushed past. She framed these choices as sensible, temporary, even healthy. Yet by turning away from the very cues that evoked the memory, and by shutting down any thought that was not reassuring, she left the experience preserved in the same broken pieces. Nothing had a chance to become more complete; the event remained a set of intrusions and absences rather than a past crisis she could place in context.

The more she relied on these habits, the more estranged she felt from herself. Her relentless private search for why this happened never yielded an answer that satisfied her, and her forced positivity only deepened her sense that she was performing a version of Mereana she no longer believed in. Avoiding medical reminders also carried a humiliation she could not ignore. A surgeon who once walked into trauma bays without hesitation now found herself timing her route through the hospital to miss ambulance arrivals. That discrepancy fed her conviction that something fundamental had been lost. She had come to feel that the illness had not only endangered her life but stripped away the self she trusted, and with that came a broader loss of faith—in the body, in the predictability of life, even in the meanings she had once used to steady herself.

She finally sought help after recognizing that her world had narrowed around these efforts to cope. Colleagues had noticed her reluctance to be near certain parts of the hospital, and she had begun wondering whether she should stop operating altogether. What frightened her most was not simply remembering the illness, but the possibility that she would remain divided from herself indefinitely: a doctor who could not bear the cues of medicine, a woman trying to think positively while privately feeling blank, fragmented, and altered beyond recognition. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not just relief from fear but a way to understand what happened without disappearing inside it.
